Tomato___Early_blight.description: Early blight is a common fungal disease causing concentric dark rings ('target spots') on older leaves first, gradually progressing upwards.
symptoms: Dark brown to black spots with concentric rings on lower leaves
Yellow halo surrounding the leaf lesions
Premature leaf drop exposing fruits to sunscald
Dark, sunken lesions on stems near the soil line
causes: Warm temperatures (24°C to 29°C) accompanied by wet weather or high humidity
Fungal spores surviving in diseased plant debris in soil
Overhead irrigation splashing fungal spores onto lower foliage
organic_treatment: Prune affected lower leaves immediately and dispose away from garden
Apply copper octanoate or copper sulfate liquid sprays
Spray bio-fungicides containing Bacillus subtilis
Apply thick organic mulch (straw or bark) to prevent soil splashing
chemical_treatment: Apply fungicides containing Chlorothalonil or Mancozeb every 7-10 days during wet periods
Alternate with azoxystrobin to prevent chemical resistance
prevention: Practice 3-year crop rotation with non-solanaceous crops
Use drip irrigation rather than overhead sprinklers to keep foliage dry
Stake and cage tomato plants to improve air circulation

Tomato___Late_blight.description: A devastating water mold that caused the Irish Potato Famine. Spreads rapidly in cool, moist weather, destroying foliage and fruit in days.
symptoms: Water-soaked irregular pale-green or brown lesions on leaves
White fuzzy mold growth on the undersides of leaves in humid conditions
Rapid browning and collapse of entire leaf branches
Large firm brown lesions on tomato fruits
causes: Cool, rainy, or foggy weather (15°C to 20°C with 90%+ relative humidity)
Windborne spores traveling long distances across fields
Infected volunteer tomato or potato seedlings
organic_treatment: Remove and bag infected plants immediately; do NOT compost infected material
Preventive sprays of fixed copper fungicide prior to wet weather
Keep plants under transparent protective rain covers in high-risk zones
chemical_treatment: Preventive systemic fungicides such as metalaxyl, cymoxanil, or dimethomorph
Contact protectants like chlorothalonil applied ahead of rainy weather
prevention: Plant certified disease-resistant tomato varieties (e.g., Defiant, Mountain Magic)
Ensure wide plant spacing for rapid leaf drying after rain
Eradicate nearby wild solanaceous weeds

Tomato___healthy.description: The leaf exhibits vibrant green chlorophyll, intact venation, and zero signs of pathogen infestation or nutritional deficiency.
symptoms: Uniform green foliage without discoloration or necrosis
Firm, well-hydrated leaf turgor
No spotting, wilting, curling, or mildew
causes: Balanced soil nutrients (N-P-K and trace minerals)
Adequate sunlight and proper moisture management
organic_treatment: Continue standard organic fertilization (compost tea, vermicompost)
Maintain 2-3 inches of clean organic mulch around base
chemical_treatment: No chemical fungicides or bactericides required
prevention: Maintain regular drip irrigation schedule
Scout leaves weekly for early signs of pests or spotting
Ensure 6-8 hours of direct daily sunlight

Potato___Early_blight.description: Fungal infection creating brown target-shaped spots with concentric rings on potato foliage, impairing tuber yield.
symptoms: Dark brown circular to angular spots with concentric concentric rings
Yellowing chlorosis around the lesions
Lower leaves drop prematurely, weakening tuber development
causes: Stressed plants due to nitrogen deficiency or moisture fluctuations
Warm days with high humidity and wet nights
organic_treatment: Apply neem oil extracts or copper-based fungicides
Mulch soil to reduce spore splash
chemical_treatment: Spray mancozeb, chlorothalonil, or pyraclostrobin upon first detection
prevention: Maintain optimal nitrogen fertility to preserve vine vitality
Rotate with non-solanaceous crops such as legumes or corn

Potato___Late_blight.description: Aggressive disease that damages foliage and causes foul-smelling dry rot inside developing potato tubers.
symptoms: Dark water-soaked spots that turn purplish-brown
White fungal-like fuzz on lower leaf surface in morning dew
Stems show greasy brown lesions; foliage wilts rapidly
causes: Prolonged leaf wetness and cool ambient temperatures (12°C - 22°C)
organic_treatment: Immediately cull and safely destroy all infected foliage
Apply protective copper hydroxide sprays
chemical_treatment: Systemic fungicides like cymoxanil, propamocarb, or fluopicolide
prevention: Plant only certified disease-free seed tubers
Hill up soil well around potato bases to protect tubers from surface spores

Potato___healthy.description: Potato foliage is crisp, healthy, and synthesizing carbohydrates actively for underground tuber bulking.
symptoms: Rich green leaf color with smooth leaf margins
Stems are sturdy and erect with no rotting or lesions
causes: Adequate soil moisture and well-drained fertile soil
organic_treatment: Provide light potassium-rich compost to support tuber bulking
prevention: Keep soil evenly moist without waterlogging
Perform periodic hilling up of soil around root zone

Corn_(maize)___Common_rust.description: Fungal rust creating reddish-brown pustules across corn leaf blades, inhibiting photosynthesis in grain crops.
symptoms: Oval to elongate cinnamon-brown powdery pustules on both leaf surfaces
Pustules rupture epidermal tissue releasing reddish spores
Severe infections lead to leaf chlorosis and premature senescence
causes: Wind-blown spores from southern climates, cool temperatures (16°C - 25°C), and high humidity
organic_treatment: Apply sulfur dust or bio-fungicide sprays early in season
Remove lower infected corn leaf remnants
chemical_treatment: Apply triazole or strobilurin fungicides if rust emerges before tasseling
prevention: Plant rust-resistant corn hybrid seeds
Early planting to avoid peak seasonal spore migration

Corn_(maize)___healthy.description: The maize blade shows robust venation, deep green color, and high photosynthetic vigour.
symptoms: Smooth, broad, bright green leaf surfaces
No pustules, stripes, or necrotic edges
causes: Optimal nitrogen uptake and warm sunny climate
organic_treatment: Balanced side-dressing with organic matter
prevention: Ensure sufficient soil nitrogen and well-spaced rows

Pepper__bell___Bacterial_spot.description: Bacterial infection causing necrotic spots on leaves and fruit, causing severe defoliation in pepper crops.
symptoms: Small, yellowish-green lesions turning water-soaked and dark brown
Lesions with slightly raised margins or dead centers that drop out
Extensive leaf shedding leaving pepper fruit susceptible to sunscald
causes: Warm rainy weather, overhead watering, and contaminated seeds
organic_treatment: Apply fixed copper mixed with organic bactericides
Sanitize pruning tools between plants
chemical_treatment: Copper hydroxide paired with mancozeb for improved bacterial suppression
prevention: Use hot-water treated or certified disease-free seeds
Avoid handling pepper plants when leaves are wet

Pepper__bell___healthy.description: Vibrant bell pepper leaf with smooth cuticle, bright green hue, and no microbial lesions.
symptoms: Glossy green leaves with uniform surface
Normal flowering and healthy shoot tips
organic_treatment: Apply organic fish emulsion or seaweed extract
prevention: Mulch soil bed and water at the root zone

Apple___Apple_scab.description: Prevalent fungal disease causing olive-green to black velvety spots on apple leaves and scabby lesions on apples.
symptoms: Olive-green velvety spots on leaf tops that turn dark brown/black
Leaves become distorted, puckered, and drop prematurely
Corky scab lesions on developing fruits
causes: Wet spring weather with continuous moisture on leaves for 6+ hours
organic_treatment: Spray sulfur or copper soap spray prior to blossom opening
Rake and compost fallen leaves thoroughly in autumn
chemical_treatment: Myclobutanil, captan, or mancozeb applied during bud break and bloom
prevention: Plant scab-resistant cultivars (e.g., Liberty, Prima, Freedom)
Prune canopy regularly to increase sunlight penetration and aeration

Apple___healthy.description: Healthy apple leaf with strong chlorophyll synthesis, clear venation, and intact margins.
symptoms: Deep green, serrated leaf margins without blemishes
Strong petiole attachment to branches
causes: Good soil aeration, winter pruning, and proper pest management
organic_treatment: Standard balanced organic orchard management
prevention: Maintain clean orchard floor and monitor seasonal weather
